title.value: The Dark Side of Scale: Insecurity of Direct-to-Cell Satellite Mega-Constellations
The Dark Side of Scale: Insecurity of Direct-to-Cell Satellite Mega-Constellations

abstract.value: The emergent direct-to-cell Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite mega-constellations promise ubiquitous LTE/5G access for our commodity phones and IoTs without terrestrial base stations. While their extreme scale and mobility help tolerate diverse attacks, we show that both new features are exploitable to amplify signaling protocol vulnerabilities inherited from LTE/5G and obfuscate attacks to threaten satellite services. We showcase this with SatOver, a control-plane cross-layer attack that lets a greedy terrestrial operator or a man-inthe-middle attacker block all direct-to-cell satellites in urban areas. SatOver can reuse terrestrial LTE/5G base stations or deploy commodity software-defined radios as false satellites, stealthily hijack victim devices, delay their satellite access, stop them from probing other satellites, and block the entire mega-constellation. Our real-world satellite tests, lab tests with commodity 3GPP NR/IoT-NTN stacks, and operational tracedriven emulation validate SatOver's viability for attacking COTS and upcoming NTN phones/IoTs. We discuss potential defenses against SatOver's attack amplification/obfuscation.

The emergent direct-to-cell Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite mega-constellations promise ubiquitous LTE/5G access for our commodity phones and IoTs without terrestrial base stations. While their extreme scale and mobility help tolerate diverse attacks, we show that both new features are exploitable to amplify signaling protocol vulnerabilities inherited from LTE/5G and obfuscate attacks to threaten satellite services. We showcase this with SatOver, a control-plane cross-layer attack that lets a greedy terrestrial operator or a man-in- the-middle attacker block all direct-to-cell satellites in urban areas. SatOver can reuse terrestrial LTE/5G base stations or deploy commodity software-defined radios as false satellites, stealthily hijack victim devices, delay their satellite access, stop them from probing other satellites, and block the entire mega-constellation. Our real-world satellite tests, lab tests with commodity 3GPP NR/IoT-NTN stacks, and operational trace- driven emulation validate SatOver's viability for attacking COTS and upcoming NTN phones/IoTs. We discuss potential defenses against SatOver's attack amplification/obfuscation. 1. Introduction Space is the next frontier for mobile networks. The emergent direct-to-cell satellites extend terrestrial LTE/5G to space and promise direct network access for our regular phones and IoT devices in rural areas, airplanes, oceans, and other dead zones. Recent Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) mega- constellations, such as Starlink [1], [2], Iridium [3], [4], Globalstar [5], and Inmarsat [6], further place satellites closer to devices for better radio quality, faster network speed, and cheaper hardware. Since 2022, direct-to-cell satellites have gained traction from operators [1], [7], [8], phone/IoT vendors [3], [9]-[12], and standards [13]-[22]. Direct-to-cell satellites are a double-edged sword for ter- restrial mobile operators. While optimizing terrestrial mobile operators' costs and revenues in rural areas, they can also spur unforeseen competition for subscribers between local and foreign operators in urban areas ( §2.3). This concern has been recently raised by terrestrial telecom operators in many countries in the world [23]-[29]. Since LEO mega- constellations are unavoidably exposed to foreign regions, it is open to question if they are at risk of attacks by greedy terrestrial operators for unfair competition or protectionism. At first glimpse, this concern seems overcautious. Unlike traditional standalone geostationary satellites, LEO mega- PhoneCOTS Core Network Internet PhoneNTN Radio Access Network NASNTN RRCNTN NAS RRC NASNTN NAS Satphone NAS RRC NAS IoTNTN NASNTN RRCNTN NASNTN Base station Ground station LEO-NRNTN RRC station RCCCCCCCCCC RRCNTN C NTN GEO RRC RC RRCNTN NTN RRC ase sta LEO LEO - NR NTN LEO LEO-IoTNTN Figure 1: Direct-to-cell LTE/5G satellite network. constellations seem already resilient to attacks due to their extreme mobility and scale. Each LEO satellite is a fast- moving target at ≈7km/s, thus only exposing short-lived visibility and attack surfaces for adversaries. Moreover, attacking one satellite does not suffice to threaten the en- tire mega-constellation, whose 100s-1,000s satellites offer abundant backups to tolerate attacks. Both have been ev- idenced in the recent Russia-Ukraine conflict [30], where Starlink rapidly fought off Russian radio jamming attacks. Our empirical analysis in §3 also confirms the LEO mega- constellation's robustness to classic satellite attacks. This paper makes a case to challenge the above myth with SatOver, a control-plane cross-layer attack that lets a greedy terrestrial LTE/5G operator or a man-in-the-middle attacker block direct-to-cell mega-constellations in urban areas (e.g., for protectionism). It observes that, for com- patibility with commodity phones/IoTs, direct-to-cell satel- lites inherit terrestrial LTE/5G protocols that suffer from plaintext broadcast and registration signalings. While ter- restrial attacks [31]-[38] have also exploited similar vul- nerabilities, they do not suffice to block the entire mega- constellation due to limited attack scopes or straightforward mitigations (§3.2). Instead, SatOver exploits the LEO mega- constellation's extreme scale and mobility to amplify and obfuscate unauthentic signalings for successful attacks: •Attack amplification by exploiting scale: Direct-to- cell satellites rely on centralized ground stations to process all users' LTE/5G signaling, thus leading to control-plane congestions due to the mega-constellation nature [39]-[41]. SatOver leverages this to mimic signaling congestions and stealthily delay victims' service requests that, unlike [31]- [34], can implicitly block the entire mega-constellation. •Attack obfuscation by exploiting mobility: SatOver obfuscates its attacks via rapid RF, geometric, and protocol 445 DOI 10.1109/SP54263.2024.00149 GEO Altitude: 35,786km RTT: 240ms LEO mega-constellation Altitude: 340km-2000km RTT: 2-12ms (a) Satellite, mega-constellation, and their coverage/performance Satellites Total Total Altitude Speed Mobile per orbit orbits satellites H (km) (km/s) technology Starlink [1], [2] 22 72 1,584 340/550 7.6 LTE Iridium [3], [4] 11 6 66 780 7.4 5G Globalstar [5] 6 8 48 1,414 7.2 CDMA/5G Inmarsat [6] 18 11 198 1,023.5 7.3 5G OneWeb [42] 40 18 720 1,200 7.3 LTE/5G (b) Scale and mobility of operational LEO mega-constellations Figure 2: Direct-to-cell LEO satellite mega-constellations. forgery and reconfigurations. This strategy disguises one attacker as many fast-changing satellites in real LEO mega- constellations, thus making it tricky for victims to defend. With both ideas, SatOver can reuse terrestrial LTE/5G base stations or deploy commodity software-defined radios as “false satellites” to stealthily hijack end devices, delay their satellite services, stop them from searching for other satellites, and block the entire satellite mega-constellation. SatOver can threaten most standard-compliant smartphones and IoTs that access satellites via 3G, 4G LTE, and 5G. It is scalable and incrementally deployable to greedy operators' massive terrestrial base stations with marginal impacts on their legitimate cellular services, thus further offsetting the LEO mega-constellation's scale advantages. Our real-world satellite tests, lab tests with Amarisoft's commodity 3GPP non-terrestrial network (NTN) stack, and operational trace- driven emulation validate SatOver's viability in attacking both the commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) phones and up- coming IoT/NR-NTN devices ( §5). We further discuss how to counteract SatOver's attack amplifications and obfuscations for a robust and practical defense ( §6). We show that, while each device cannot easily combat SatOver, it is possible to detect and mitigate SatOver based on the time difference of the false satellite's signal arrivals to different victims. We discuss how to realize so in practice, analyze its security, and validate its feasibility. 2. Direct-to-Cell Satellite Mega-Constellations We review the terrestrial mobile network's limitations (§2.1), motivate direct-to-cell mega-constellations ( §2.2), and discuss their cooperation/competition in reality ( §2.3). 2.1. Terrestrial Mobile Network and Limitations LTE/5G mobile network is the largest terrestrial wireless infrastructure to offer wide-area network access for billions of phones and IoTs. It consists of a radio access network and a core network (Figure 1). The radio access network comprises massive base stations, each covering a geographic area to connect user equipments (UEs) wirelessly. The core network bridges base stations and the external Internet. To facilitate traffic delivery, LTE/5G adopts layered signaling protocols: The base station runs radio resource control 960 l l 5150 5925MHz16261428 2300 2483 27001805 2100617 410 466MHz427 450 410 LTE band covered by SpaceX filings LTE band not covered by SpaceX filings LTE band partly covered by SpaceX filings Non-LTE band Figure 3: LTE radio bands covered by SpaceX Starlink's ITU filings for its direct-to-cell LEO satellites [47], [48]. (RRC), while the core network manages the UE mobility and session with its non-access stratum (NAS) protocols. Despite its great success, terrestrial LTE/5G still suf- fers from limited coverage, exhaustive capital costs, and disasters. Its terrestrial base stations are not ubiquitously available, thus leaving service black holes for 3.7 billion unconnected users [43] and numerous IoT sensors in rural areas, airplanes, and oceans. Covering these dead zones requires billions of dollars of investments for operators to adopt terrestrial infrastructure [44]. Unexpected natural disasters [45] or wars [46] can easily disrupt these infras- tructure. All these issues motivate operators to complement their terrestrial network with low-cost, resilient infrastruc- ture with broad coverage, such as direct-to-cell satellites. 2.2. From Terrestrial to Space Mobile Network Direct-to-cell communication satellites have been opera- tional since the 2G era [49]-[54]. Traditionally, they operate in the geostationary orbit (GEO) at the altitude of 35,786km for broad coverage. Due to their distant radio propagations and path loss, GEO satellites are only accessible by dedi- cated satphones with high-gain antennas, thus limiting their availability and affordability to most customers. Instead, LEO satellites [1]-[6] eliminate this technical barrier. They reside at 340- 2000km altitudes, hence 10- 100× closer to users than GEO satellites. Our commodity phones and IoT devices can directly access them without dedicated high-end antenna. Due to each LEO satellite's smaller coverage, the LEO (mega-)constellations have been link partnered with T-Mobile to offer direct-to-cell satellite services [1]. To facilitate the collaboration with international mobile operators, Starlink has applied for most LTE radio bands for its satellites [47], [48] (Figure 3 and Table 3). Ap- ple has partnered with Globalstar to offer direct-to-satellite emergency SOS for iPhone 14 and above [5], while Qual- comm's Snapdragon Satellite modem using the Iridium LEO constellation will be available in Android phones soon [3]. Both narrowband IoT and broadband direct-to-cell satellites are under field trials and standardization [13]-[17]. As an extension to terrestrial mobile networks, direct-to- cell satellites reuse LTE/5G protocols with mild customiza- tions (Figure 1). There are two variants. For our unmodified COTS phones/IoTs, satellites like Starlink [2], AST [55], and Lynk [56] can directly connect them by mimicking themselves as terrestrial base stations. The cost, however, is the increased satellite complexity (hence increasing satellite manufacturing launching costs) and phone battery drains. In- stead, 3GPP is extending its standards to non-terrestrial net- works (NTN [13]-[22]) for narrowband Internet-of-Things (IoT-NTN) and broadband 5G new radio (NR-NTN). It 446
